title: Woman Develops Severe Brain Disorder After 15-Day Water-Only Diet, May Never Walk Normally Again
excerpt: Doctors diagnose Wernicke's encephalopathy after a Chinese woman's extreme fast depleted her vitamin B1 reserves, leaving her with a 'penguin-like' gait that may be permanent.
body:
• A 31-year-old woman in China's Henan province developed Wernicke's encephalopathy — a severe brain disorder — after a 15-day water-only fast that dropped her weight from 70 kg to 50 kg
  • Neurologist Sun Guifang says the woman now walks with a permanent "penguin-like" gait caused by critical vitamin B1 (thiamine) depletion
  • The fast was part of "bigu," a traditional Taoist practice meaning "grain avoidance" that has gained traction on social media as a weight-loss trend
  • Medical research shows Wernicke's encephalopathy has a 17% mortality rate, with 80% of survivors developing Korsakoff syndrome, a condition marked by severe memory impairment

A 31-year-old woman from Henan province in China has developed a severe and potentially irreversible brain disorder after undertaking a 15-day water-only fast, according to doctors at The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University.

The woman, who has not been publicly identified, lost approximately 20 kilograms — dropping from 70 kg to 50 kg — during the extreme fast. She was subsequently diagnosed with Wernicke's encephalopathy, an acute neurological condition triggered by a critical deficiency of vitamin B1, also known as thiamine.

A Walk That May Never Recover

Neurologist Sun Guifang, who treated the woman, told Chinese media that her gait now resembles that of a "penguin" — a distinctive wide-based, unsteady walk characteristic of cerebellar damage. Dr. Sun warned the condition may prove irreversible.

Beyond the walking impairment, the woman suffered severe memory deterioration. Medical records indicate she struggled to recall basic recent events and showed signs of confusion consistent with the early stages of Korsakoff syndrome, a chronic condition that frequently follows Wernicke's encephalopathy.

How 15 Days Without Food Damages the Brain

The medical timeline aligns precisely with established research on thiamine depletion. According to StatPearls, a medical database maintained by the U.S. National Institutes of Health, the body's thiamine stores are exhausted within approximately two weeks when intake is restricted. A 2007 study by researchers Sechi and Serra documented that brain lesions begin forming between two and three weeks of deficiency, particularly in the mammillary bodies — brain structures that consume large amounts of thiamine.

Thiamine is a water-soluble vitamin, meaning the body stores very little of it. It serves as an essential coenzyme in the metabolic pathways through which the brain converts glucose into energy. When stores are depleted, brain cells effectively starve, even if the rest of the body has sufficient energy reserves.

"Undertaking prolonged starvation without medical oversight poses severe risks to vital organ systems and neurological stability."

— Dr. Rajeev Chowdry, Director of Internal Medicine, Yatharth Hospital, Faridabad

The Bigu Trend on Social Media

The woman's fast was reportedly part of "bigu," a traditional Taoist practice that translates to "abstaining from grains." Historically, practitioners aimed to purify the body or achieve spiritual enlightenment by forgoing staple foods for extended periods. The practice has gained renewed popularity on Chinese social media platforms, where users share dramatic before-and-after weight loss results.

Medical experts warn that the spiritual interpretations of bigu do not account for the severe physiological risks of prolonged fasting. When the body is deprived of food beyond a few days, it exhausts glycogen reserves and begins breaking down both fat tissue and lean muscle mass. The rapid weight loss visible on a scale reflects not just fat reduction, but acute depletion of fluids, glycogen, and essential muscle tissue.

A Warning for Extreme Dieters

The prognosis for Wernicke's encephalopathy is grim. StatPearls reports a mortality rate of 17%, with 80% of survivors progressing to Korsakoff syndrome — a condition characterized by severe, often permanent memory impairment. Autopsy studies have found a prevalence of 1% to 3% in the general population, while the rate of diagnosis during a patient's lifetime stands at approximately 20%, suggesting many cases go unrecognized.

The case underscores a growing global concern about extreme fasting trends promoted without medical oversight. Health authorities in multiple countries have warned against water-only fasts lasting more than 24 to 48 hours without professional supervision, noting that the risks extend far beyond weight loss to include organ damage, cardiac complications, and irreversible neurological harm.
